311.quote_or_event: Macauliffe records that at Saiyidpur (Eminabad) Guru Nanak lodged with Lalo, a low-caste carpenter, and declined the great feast of Malik Bhago, the local steward. When Malik Bhago demanded why, the Guru took Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Bhago's rich bread in the other and squeezed them: it is said milk came from Lalo's bread and blood from Bhago's, because Bhago's wealth had been gained by bribery and oppression.
311.explanation: The story, from the Janamsakhi tradition as Macauliffe retells it, sets honest poverty above lavish wealth that was squeezed out of other people's suffering. Guru Nanak refuses the rich man's hospitality outright.
311.tie_back: The Kural says the stainless will not cause pain even for wealth that brings great prestige; Guru Nanak turned away from just such prestigious wealth because it had been gained by hurting others.
311.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 43-44 (paraphrase)
311._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on refusing wealth gained through others' pain. The milk-and-blood detail is hagiography from the Janamsakhi tradition, which Macauliffe himself introduces with 'it is said'.

312.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
312.explanation: In one of his saloks preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the seeker not to hit back at those who strike him, but to answer with humility and return to inner peace.
312.tie_back: The Kural asks the stainless not to hurt in return even those who have spitefully hurt them; Farid gives the same rule in its most physical form, a blow received and not returned.
312.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
312._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on refusing retaliation. The words are Sheikh Farid's, a Sufi saint whose verses are included in the Sikh scripture, not a Sikh Guru's.

313.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and I am no one's enemy.”
313.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy: enmity has gone from both sides, because he no longer answers hostility with hostility.
313.tie_back: The Kural warns that striking back even at those who hated us without cause brings sorrow; Guru Arjan describes the freedom of one who has stopped being anyone's enemy.
313.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 671, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
313._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the verse describes freedom from enmity in general and does not speak of unprovoked hatred or of the grief that retaliation brings, which are the Kural's specific points.

314.quote_or_event: “A noble person does not adopt demerits in his heart and does good to the evil doer.”
314.explanation: In a stanza titled 'good and bad', Bhai Gurdas compares the noble person to madder, which bears the heat yet dyes others fast, and to sugarcane, which grows sweeter the more it is crushed. Bhai Gurdas's Vaaran are early and authoritative Sikh exegesis, not scripture.
314.tie_back: The Kural's way to punish wrongdoers is to do them good and let the matter go; Bhai Gurdas likewise praises the one who answers evil with good and keeps no grievance in the heart.
314.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 31, Pauri 15 (English translation as given in the BaniDB database)
314._accuracy_note: A strong fit on repaying evil with good and letting it go; Bhai Gurdas does not mention the wrongdoer's shame, which is the Kural's distinctive touch.

315.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being delights in doing good to others.”
315.explanation: In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes the brahm giani, the person of true spiritual knowledge, and makes active kindness to others one of the marks of that knowledge.
315.tie_back: The Kural asks what use knowledge is if it does not make another's pain one's own; for Guru Arjan the highest knowledge shows itself precisely in doing good to others.
315.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 273, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
315._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it links true knowledge with beneficence, but does not frame it as feeling another's pain as one's own or as a test of learning.

316.quote_or_event: “As you see yourself, see others as well; only then will you become a partner in heaven.”
316.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, addressing the religious authorities of his day, makes seeing others as oneself the condition of true religion.
316.tie_back: The Kural's rule is not to do to others what one has felt as painful oneself; Kabir grounds the same rule in seeing others exactly as one sees oneself.
316.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 480, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
316._accuracy_note: A strong Golden Rule parallel; Kabir states it positively (see others as yourself) rather than as the Kural's negative rule drawn from one's own experience of pain, and he is a Bhagat in the Granth, not a Guru.

317.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all. Do not break anyone's heart; these are all priceless jewels.”
317.explanation: Sheikh Farid forbids even the smallest hurt, a single harsh word, because God dwells in every person and every heart is precious.
317.tie_back: The Kural calls it the highest virtue never to cause harm to anyone, however slight; Farid likewise forbids harm down to one unkind word, to anyone at all.
317.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 129 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
317._accuracy_note: A strong fit on universal and minimal harm; Farid speaks of words and hearts rather than the Kural's explicit inclusion of harm in thought.

318.quote_or_event: “You say that the One Lord is in all, so why do you kill chickens?”
318.explanation: Kabir exposes the contradiction in someone who professes that God dwells in every creature yet takes a creature's life.
318.tie_back: The Kural asks why one who knows pain in one's own life inflicts it on other lives; Kabir's question likewise exposes the self-contradiction in harming beings one admits are like oneself.
318.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
318._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both use a rhetorical 'why?' against harming living beings, but Kabir argues from God's presence in all (and targets ritual slaughter), not from one's own experience of pain.

319.explanation: In the Japji, Guru Nanak states the law of action plainly: what a person sows in deeds, that same person reaps.
319.tie_back: The Kural warns that harm done in the morning returns to the doer by afternoon; Guru Nanak teaches the same return of one's deeds to oneself.
319.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
319._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the same law of return, but without the Kural's striking compression of time into a single day.

320.quote_or_event: “Do not harbor evil intentions against others in your mind, and you shall not be troubled, O Siblings of Destiny, O friends.”
320.explanation: Guru Arjan ties freedom from one's own trouble directly to not wishing harm on others.
320.tie_back: The Kural concludes that those who wish to be free of suffering do not cause it to others; Guru Arjan gives the same practical counsel: wish no one harm, and harm will not trouble you.
320.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
320._accuracy_note: Close to one-to-one on the conditional (do no harm, suffer none); the Kural's first line, that all suffering falls on those who cause it, is only implied.
